languages: Gothic, lost to Latin within a few generations in Hispania

imageInfo.note: A nineteenth-century imagining commissioned for the Spanish Senate, not a record of the council: the costume, the architecture and the staging are the painter's. It is also a document of how the 589 conversion was later used, since the nationalist reading of that council as the birth of Catholic Spain is exactly what a painting in a parliament building was built to assert. Public domain.

summary: The Visigoths formed inside the Roman empire between 376 and 418, sacked Rome in 410, and ruled a kingdom from Toulouse and then Toledo that produced the earliest surviving Germanic law code and lasted until 711.
overview: A people made on the wrong side of a river crossing, who ended up legislating for everyone in Spain.
knownFor: Formed as a people inside the Roman empire between the Danube crossing of 376 and the settlement of 418.
Sacked Rome over three days in August 410, prompting Augustine to begin The City of God.
Issued the Codex Euricianus of about 475, the earliest surviving Germanic law code.
Abandoned Arian Christianity for the Nicene faith of their subjects at Toledo in 589.
Made law territorial in 654, applying one code to Goth and Roman alike.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The Visigoths came together inside the Roman empire between the Danube crossing of 376 and the Aquitaine settlement of 418, and ruled a kingdom for nearly three centuries — from Toulouse, and after 507 from Toledo. They are the Gothic people who solved the problem the other one did not: the religious and legal division between a Gothic military elite and a far larger Roman population, closed deliberately, by dated acts, between 580 and 654.

The kingdom ended abruptly when Roderic was killed in 711 and Toledo fell. The Liber Iudiciorum was still used in Iberian courts as the Fuero Juzgo six hundred years later, and northern Iberian kings spent centuries claiming to be the Goths' heirs. The polity lasted three hundred years; the claim to be its successor lasted twice that.

contentSections.title: Names and Identity
paragraphs: The Visigoths had no distinct endonym: they called themselves Goths. Visigothi is not a name they used of themselves in the fourth century — it appears as a fixed term with Cassiodorus, paired with Ostrogothi as a matched set of "western" and "eastern" Goths, and Jordanes passed the arrangement on to everyone who read him afterwards.

Modern scholars generally reject the compass-point etymology. Vesi or Visi, which does appear in fourth-century Latin sources such as the Notitia Dignitatum and in Claudian, is treated as the older and possibly self-applied name, perhaps "the good" or "the noble" Goths. The tidy western-and-eastern pairing is a sixth-century literary convenience laid over two peoples who formed separately and at different times.

Ammianus' name for the group north of the lower Danube in the fourth century is Tervingi. Equating Tervingi with Visigoths is useful shorthand and inexact in a way that matters: the people who received land in Aquitaine in 418 included Greuthungi, Alans and others absorbed during forty years of movement and war.

The scholarly disagreement is sharpest here. Kulikowski argues that the Visigoths were created inside the empire and that a distinct pre-Danube Visigothic people is a retrojection from later sources. Heather allows more continuity, seeing a Tervingian core that held through 376 and re-formed around Alaric. Wolfram proposes a Traditionskern, a leading group carrying genuine tradition that others joined. Halsall and Pohl stress that the identity was situational, asserted more strongly at some moments than others. All of them accept that the years from 376 to 418 were formative; what they dispute is how much existed before them.

contentSections.title: Made inside the empire, 376 to 418
paragraphs: The Visigoths originate as a political community in the crisis of 376, not in Scandinavia. Tervingi under Fritigern and Alavivus crossed the Danube under Hunnic pressure; Roman mismanagement of the refugees turned them into an army; Adrianople in 378 gave them a bargaining position no barbarian group had held before; and the treaty of 382 gave them a legal existence inside the empire.

Consolidation came under Alaric I, raised as king in 395, who welded the treaty Goths and others into a force neither imperial court could ignore. Stilicho checked his Italian campaigns at Pollentia in 402 and Verona in 403, but three blockades of Rome from 408 ended in the sack of 24 to 27 August 410, which prompted Augustine to begin The City of God. Alaric died in southern Italy later the same year.

Athaulf moved the Goths into Gaul and married the emperor's sister Galla Placidia at Narbonne in 414, in a ceremony staged with deliberate Roman propriety — a bid for Gothic-Roman fusion at the highest possible level. Wallia then campaigned in Spain against Vandals and Alans on Rome's behalf, and the settlement of 418 in Aquitania Secunda made the Goths a people with land, a capital at Toulouse and a frontier. Expansion under Euric from 466 took most of southern Gaul and much of Hispania; it reversed at Vouillé in 507, where Clovis killed Alaric II and pushed the kingdom south of the Pyrenees for good.

contentSections.title: The settlement question: land or tax revenue
paragraphs: One mechanism at the heart of the settlement is genuinely unresolved. The traditional view is that the Goths received real shares of land, sortes, taken from Roman proprietors — a dispossession, however orderly, of the existing landowning class.

Walter Goffart argued in 1980 that they instead received assignments of tax revenue, which would make the settlement an administrative act carried out through the existing fiscal machinery rather than a transfer of estates. The debate is unsettled, and not a technicality: the two models imply completely different relationships between the incoming Gothic elite and the Roman landowners they lived among.

The consequences run through everything else here. If the Goths took land, the Hispano-Roman aristocracy had a standing grievance and the later fusion of the two populations is more surprising than it looks. If they took revenue, the settlement gave the Roman landowning class a reason to keep the fiscal system running and the Gothic elite a reason to protect it. The same uncertainty applies to the Gothic settlement in Italy.

contentSections.title: Kingship and its recurring crisis
paragraphs: Visigothic kingship was elective in principle and violently contested in practice. Gregory of Tours called king-killing the morbus Gothorum, the disease of the Goths, and the record broadly supports him: a substantial proportion of Visigothic kings were deposed or murdered, and no dynasty established itself securely enough to make succession routine.

After 589 the institution that tried to fix this was the Councils of Toledo, which combined bishops with the lay magnates of the palace and legislated on secular as well as church matters. The Fourth Council of 633, presided over by Isidore of Seville, regulated royal election, condemned usurpation and bound the nobility by oath. It was an attempt to solve a political problem by making the church the guarantor of legitimacy.

It worked imperfectly, and the cost was structural: the monarchy became dependent on episcopal and aristocratic consent for its legitimacy, so a king who lost the confidence of the councils lost the argument about whether he was lawfully king at all. Administration ran on late Roman lines throughout — an officium palatinum of household officers, dukes over provinces and counts over cities — so the instability sat at the top of an otherwise functioning structure.

contentSections.title: Two churches in one kingdom
paragraphs: Until 589 the kingdom contained two complete and parallel churches. The Homoian church of the Goths had its own bishops, clergy and baptism, and it rebaptised converts coming from the Nicene church — the practice that made the division a fact of ordinary experience rather than a dispute among theologians. The Hispano-Roman population was Nicene, with its own long-established hierarchy, wealth and networks.

The political cost was continuous. A Gothic king could not be the religious head of most of his subjects; Nicene bishops were natural channels for a hostile foreign power, which mattered increasingly once the eastern empire held the south-eastern coast from 552; and any Gothic dissident could acquire a ready-made constituency by changing sides in the religious argument.

Every serious crisis of the sixth century ran along that line. The kingdom that emerged after 589 was not more religious than the one before; it was one in which rulers and ruled could belong to the same institution.

contentSections.title: Leovigild, Hermenegild and the collision of 579 to 584
paragraphs: Leovigild, who ruled from 569 to 586, tried to close the gap on Arian terms. At a council in Toledo in 580 he dropped the requirement that Nicene converts be rebaptised, hoping to make joining the Gothic church cheap. It failed in both directions: his own clergy read the concession as weakness, everyone else as insufficient.

His son Hermenegild revolted between 579 and 584, having converted to Nicene Christianity, and the sources on him conflict irreconcilably. Gregory the Great presents him as a martyr for the faith. John of Biclaro and Isidore of Seville, both writing from inside the kingdom, treat him as a rebel who happened to convert. The evidence is two incompatible accounts written for different audiences, and choosing confidently between them is the commonest error in accounts of the period.

The quarrel was not purely doctrinal at court level either. Goiswintha, Leovigild's wife and previously married to Athanagild, was a formidable defender of the Gothic church and clashed violently with her Nicene granddaughter-in-law Ingund, a conflict that fed directly into the revolt.

contentSections.title: 589: the removal of the religious border
paragraphs: The resolution came from Leovigild's other son. Reccared converted, and at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 the king, the Gothic nobility and the Arian bishops formally accepted the Nicene creed — a conversion of an establishment rather than of a population, carried out in a council of the kingdom's own church.

The religious barrier between rulers and ruled disappeared, and with it the mechanism by which any discontented magnate could raise a following on doctrinal grounds. The church became the ideological backbone of the monarchy and the setting for its politics. The bishops gained a constitutional role they never afterwards surrendered, and the crown became dependent on the consent of councils it could not fully control.

One doctrinal detail from these councils carried far beyond Spain: the western career of the Filioque clause begins in the creed as professed at Toledo. A provincial settlement of a local political problem thereby contributed a phrase that would help divide the eastern and western churches centuries later.

contentSections.title: Law: from Euric's code to territorial law
paragraphs: Visigothic law is the kingdom's greatest achievement and its best-evidenced feature. The Codex Euricianus of about 475, issued by Euric, is the earliest surviving Germanic law code, written in Latin and preserved in a Paris palimpsest. It deals with property, sale, gift, loan and the division of land between Goths and Romans — practical law for a settlement that had to be made to work day by day.

The Breviarium Alaricianum, the Lex Romana Visigothorum of 506, was issued by Alaric II for his Roman subjects: an abridgement of the Theodosian Code with commentary. It became the principal channel through which Roman law reached the early medieval west, and it was used far beyond the kingdom's borders and long after its fall. Leovigild revised Euric's code in the Codex Revisus of about 580.

The decisive step was the Liber Iudiciorum of 654 under Recceswinth, revised by Erwig in 681. It was territorial law, applying to everyone in the kingdom, Goth and Roman alike, and abolishing the principle that each people carried its own law. That single change did more to fuse the two populations than any other act of the monarchy, because it removed the legal basis on which they were two populations at all.

The Liber Iudiciorum was translated into Castilian as the Fuero Juzgo in the thirteenth century under Ferdinand III and remained in use in Iberian courts for centuries, long outliving the kingdom, the dynasty and the language its first drafters spoke.

contentSections.title: The marriage ban and the making of one elite
paragraphs: For a century the Gothic military elite and the far larger Hispano-Roman population were separated by religion, by law and formally by marriage. Late Roman law prohibited marriage between Romans and barbarians, and the prohibition stood until Leovigild repealed it in about 580 — a datable step toward fusion, taken by the king who was simultaneously trying to unify the two churches on Arian terms.

After 580, 589 and 654 the distinction dissolved quickly. By the seventh century the kingdom's elite is best described as Hispano-Gothic: Gothic in name and royal tradition, Roman in law, language and church. The social hierarchy beneath it was equally mixed — the king and palatine office-holders at the top, then the seniores Gothorum whose consent made and unmade reigns, then dukes and counts, then free Goths and the Hispano-Roman landowning families who retained estates and increasingly supplied bishops, then coloni tied to the land, then slaves.

The vocabulary needs care. Neither group should be called Spanish, and the Hispano-Romans were not natives being ruled by incomers in any simple sense: both were populations of a late Roman province, and the fusion produced a provincial elite rather than a nation.

contentSections.title: Jewish communities under royal and conciliar law
paragraphs: The Jewish communities of Hispania occupied a distinct and steadily worsening position, created by specific dated royal and conciliar policy rather than by drift. Sisebut ordered forced baptism in 613. Later kings and councils legislated repeatedly against Jews and against converts suspected of insincerity, and the repetition is itself the evidence that the earlier measures had failed.

A monarchy that had solved its own religious division by a council in 589 went on to use the same instrument — king and bishops legislating together — to enforce religious uniformity on a population that had not been party to that settlement. The machinery built to end one exclusion was turned to creating another.

This legislation is among the best-documented activity of the late kingdom, because the acts of the Councils of Toledo survive. It belongs in the record as dated policy, not as background colour to a period otherwise described through kings and battles.

contentSections.title: Language: Gothic lost, and a script that is not Gothic
paragraphs: The Goths in Hispania gave up Gothic for Latin within a few generations, and the shift was close to total. What survives in Spanish is a thin layer of personal names — Rodrigo, Alfonso, Fernando, Elvira, Gonzalo, Álvaro — and a handful of common words. There is no Gothic substrate comparable to the Frankish element in French, which measures how completely the ruling group adopted the language of the ruled.

One warning belongs here, because the terminology traps almost every reader who meets it. "Visigothic script", littera visigothica, is a Latin minuscule used in Iberia from roughly the eighth to the twelfth centuries. It is not a Gothic-language script, it is not written in the alphabet Ulfilas devised, and it postdates the kingdom entirely. The name describes where the script was used, not who used it.

The Gothic language did survive in the liturgy of the Gothic church until 589, and legal and ecclesiastical Gothic is attested elsewhere in the Gothic world. In Hispania it left almost nothing, and the kingdom's entire written output — codes, council acts, chronicles, Isidore's encyclopaedia — is in Latin.

contentSections.title: Guarrazar: a king's name hung before an altar
paragraphs: The Treasure of Guarrazar, found in 1858 near Guadamur outside Toledo, is the outstanding material survival of the kingdom: votive crowns given to churches by kings and magnates, made to be hung above or before an altar rather than worn on a head.

The crown of Recceswinth carries the donor's name in pendant letters, RECCESVINTHVS REX OFFERET, in gold set with sapphires and pearls. What makes it eloquent is the grammar of the gesture: a king's name, in gold, suspended in a church as an offering. Royal authority and ecclesiastical setting are fused in the object exactly as they were fused in the Councils of Toledo.

The hoard has had a rough modern history. The crown of Suintila from the same find was stolen from the Royal Armoury in Madrid in 1921 and has never been recovered. The Torredonjimeno treasure is a comparable but more fragmentary find of the same votive type.

contentSections.title: Dress, metalwork and what the cemeteries show
paragraphs: Weapons survive less well than dress fittings, and the military kit was late Roman in derivation in any case: the spatha, the spear, the single-edged scramasax and the round shield. What actually defines Visigothic archaeology is metalwork of costume — belt buckles with rectangular plates and the great eagle fibulae of the Meseta cemeteries at Duratón, Castiltierra and El Carpio de Tajo, carrying Byzantine-influenced goldsmithing into ordinary elite dress.

A caution belongs with these objects. The label "Visigothic cemetery" has itself been questioned, and for good reason: the distinctive material marks a status group and a fashion current in the later fifth and sixth centuries, and cannot be read as a map of ethnic Gothic settlement.

The same methodological point governs the earlier Gothic material on the Danube, and it applies with more force here, because the Hispanic cemeteries have been used for more than a century to draw lines on maps. The fashion travelled; it does not follow that a people travelled with it in the proportions the grave-goods distribution suggests.

contentSections.title: Recópolis and the horseshoe arch
paragraphs: The Visigoths inherited Roman cities and built comparatively little, but what they built survives. Recópolis, founded by Leovigild in 578 and named for his son Reccared, is one of very few new cities founded anywhere in the post-Roman west. It has been excavated, and it was a deliberate statement of royal power, laid out with a palace, a church and a planned street grid.

The seventh-century churches are the other legacy: San Juan de Baños, dedicated by Recceswinth in 661 and still carrying its dedicatory inscription; San Pedro de la Nave; Santa Comba de Bande; Quintanilla de las Viñas. They are small, precisely cut stone buildings, and several of them are still standing and still roofed.

These buildings use the horseshoe arch, which is worth stating plainly because it corrects an assumption almost everyone brings to Iberian architecture: the form was current in the peninsula before the Muslim conquest, not introduced by it. A seventh-century Visigothic church is the evidence, and it predates 711 by half a century.

contentSections.title: 711 and after: the pact of Theodemir
paragraphs: The kingdom's military weakness is better documented than any account of Umayyad prowess. The army rested on royal and noble retinues supplemented by levies, and recruitment was a chronic problem: Wamba's military law of 673 penalised those who failed to answer a summons, and Erwig legislated on the same difficulty. Laws of that kind are evidence that service was being evaded.

That weakness explains 711. The kingdom had just passed through a disputed succession after Witiza's death, Roderic's accession was contested, and when he met Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād at the Guadalete a substantial part of his army had reason to want him to lose. Roderic was killed, Toledo fell, and a kingdom of three centuries collapsed within about five years — not because one battle was lost, but because an elite already split declined to fight a second one.

The best single piece of evidence for what followed is the pact of Theodemir, or Tudmir, in 713: a surviving treaty text by which a Visigothic nobleman in the south-east kept his towns, his property and the practice of his religion in return for tribute and submission. Arrangements of that kind, rather than annihilation, explain how quickly the peninsula changed hands and how much of its landowning class stayed in place.

contentSections.title: The Gothic claim, and a nationalist misuse
paragraphs: Three successor identities follow from 711. The Hispano-Gothic elite persisted under Muslim rule, and within it the Mozarab communities preserved the Visigothic liturgy and law. In the north, the kingdom of Asturias claimed the Gothic succession outright: the Chronicle of Alfonso III presents the Asturian kings as the heirs of Toledo. That neo-Gothic ideology gave León and later Castile a claim to rule the whole peninsula by inheritance rather than by conquest, and the Goths thereby became an argument in Iberian politics for another seven hundred years.

Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae was one of the most copied books of the entire Middle Ages, and his History of the Goths opens with the Laus Spaniae, the first articulation of Spain as a patria worth praising. The Councils of Toledo supplied a working model of church-and-crown government that later Iberian monarchies drew on directly.

One modern misuse should be named and rejected. The nationalist appropriation of the Visigoths as founders of a Catholic Spanish nation reads a seventh-century provincial kingdom as a nineteenth-century nation state. The 589 conversion was a political settlement as much as a religious one, and the unification of the peninsula in the 580s was a particular king solving a particular problem, not a national destiny working itself out.

timeline.title: The Danube crossing
timeline.description: Tervingi under Fritigern and Alavivus enter the empire under Hunnic pressure — the moment from which the Visigoths can be traced as a distinct political community.

timeline.title: Adrianople
timeline.description: The destruction of the eastern field army and the death of Valens give the group a bargaining position no barbarian people had previously held.

timeline.title: Alaric I made king
timeline.description: Alaric is raised as king over a following drawn from several groups, creating a unified Gothic kingship able to negotiate with both imperial courts.

timeline.title: The sack of Rome
timeline.description: Three days from 24 to 27 August, after three blockades. Alaric died in southern Italy later the same year.

timeline.title: Athaulf marries Galla Placidia
timeline.description: The marriage at Narbonne to the emperor's sister, staged with Roman propriety, was a bid for Gothic-Roman fusion at the highest level.

timeline.title: Settlement in Aquitania Secunda
timeline.description: The Goths receive a territorial settlement with Toulouse as royal seat — whether in land or in tax revenue is still disputed.

timeline.title: The Codex Euricianus
timeline.description: Euric issues the earliest surviving Germanic law code, in Latin, covering property, sale, gift, loan and the division of land between Goths and Romans.

timeline.title: The Breviary of Alaric
timeline.description: Alaric II issues the Lex Romana Visigothorum for his Roman subjects, which became the main channel carrying Roman law into the early medieval west.

timeline.title: Vouillé
timeline.description: Clovis kills Alaric II and takes Aquitaine, pushing the kingdom south of the Pyrenees permanently and moving its centre toward Toledo.

timeline.title: Recópolis founded
timeline.description: Leovigild founds a new city named for his son Reccared, one of very few founded anywhere in the post-Roman west, with a palace, a church and a planned layout.

timeline.title: The marriage ban repealed
timeline.description: Leovigild removes the late Roman prohibition on marriage between Romans and barbarians — a datable, deliberate step toward fusing the two populations.

timeline.title: Hermenegild's revolt
timeline.description: Leovigild's son revolts having converted to Nicene Christianity. Gregory the Great calls him a martyr; Isidore and John of Biclaro call him a rebel.

timeline.title: The Suevic kingdom annexed
timeline.description: Leovigild absorbs the Suevic kingdom around Braga in the north-west, completing the political unification of most of the peninsula.

timeline.title: The Third Council of Toledo
timeline.description: Reccared, the Gothic nobility and the Arian bishops accept the Nicene creed, ending the religious division between rulers and ruled.

timeline.title: Forced baptism ordered
timeline.description: Sisebut orders the forced baptism of Jews; later kings and councils legislate repeatedly on the same question, which is evidence the measures failed.

timeline.title: The Fourth Council of Toledo
timeline.description: Presided over by Isidore of Seville, it regulates royal election, condemns usurpation and binds the nobility by oath, making the church guarantor of legitimacy.

timeline.title: The Liber Iudiciorum
timeline.description: Recceswinth makes law territorial: one code for Goth and Roman alike, abolishing the principle that each people carried its own law.

timeline.title: San Juan de Baños dedicated
timeline.description: Recceswinth dedicates the church, which still carries its dedicatory inscription and uses the horseshoe arch half a century before the Muslim conquest.

timeline.title: Guadalete and the fall of Toledo
timeline.description: Roderic, whose accession was contested, is killed by Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād's forces; the kingdom collapses within about five years.

timeline.title: The pact of Theodemir
timeline.description: A surviving treaty by which a Visigothic nobleman keeps his towns, property and religion in return for tribute — the documentary proof of how the conquest actually worked.

Leovigild was the king who struck coin in his own name rather than the emperor's, and who tried in 580 to unify the two churches on Arian terms by dropping the rebaptism requirement. CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.section: 589: the removal of the religious border
sectionImages.caption: Reccared with his bishops at the Third Council of Toledo, in a miniature of about 976 from the Codex Vigilanus.
sectionImages.creator: Vigila and his fellow scribes at the monastery of Albelda
sectionImages.note: Escorial, Codex Vigilanus, fol. 145, painted nearly four centuries after the council. It is evidence of how the conversion of 589 was remembered in the Asturian-Leonese north, where the Gothic succession was being claimed, rather than of what happened in the room. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: Law: from Euric's code to territorial law
sectionImages.caption: The title page for the Theodosian Code in a Breviary of Alaric copied in 794, in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown scribe, working in 794
sectionImages.note: Cod. Sang. 731. The Breviarium Alaricianum of 506 abridged the Theodosian Code for the kingdom's Roman subjects and became the main channel carrying Roman law into the early medieval west — which is why it was still being copied in 794, long after the kingdom that issued it had gone. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: The marriage ban and the making of one elite
sectionImages.caption: A Visigothic belt plate and buckle of cast bronze with cloisonné inlay, fifth to seventh century, from the cemetery at Castiltierra in Segovia.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown metalworker; photographed by Tyk (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: the belt set fifth to seventh century; photographed 2018
sectionImages.note: Museo de Málaga. Belt sets like this from the Meseta cemeteries are what "Visigothic" archaeology in Spain actually consists of, and they mark rank and fashion rather than descent — which is this section's point, since after 580 nothing in law stopped a Hispano-Roman family marrying into that rank. CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.section: Jewish communities under royal and conciliar law
sectionImages.caption: The trilingual Hebrew, Latin and Greek epitaph from Tortosa, carved in the sixth or seventh century, in the cathedral museum there.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown carver; photographed by Enric (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: the stone sixth or seventh century; photographed 2014
sectionImages.note: One of the few surviving objects of the Jewish communities of late Roman and Visigothic Hispania, and evidence that they were long established and literate in three languages before Sisebut ordered forced baptism in 613. The dating is debated between the sixth and seventh centuries. CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.section: Language: Gothic lost, and a script that is not Gothic
sectionImages.caption: A page of the Chronicle of 754 written in Visigothic minuscule, in a copy made in the eighth or ninth century.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Iberian scribe
sectionImages.note: British Library, Egerton 1934, fol. 2r. This is littera visigothica, the Latin minuscule the section warns about: not the alphabet Ulfilas devised, not a Gothic-language script, and later than the kingdom. The chronicle itself was written by a Christian author living under Muslim rule. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: 711 and after: the pact of Theodemir
sectionImages.caption: A gold dinar struck in al-Andalus in 716 or 717, Latin on one face and Arabic on the other, photographed by Classical Numismatic Group.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Umayyad moneyer; photographed by Classical Numismatic Group
sectionImages.note: Dated AH 98 and inscribed FERITOS SOLI IN SPAN ANXCI, "struck in Spain, year 98". Bilingual coin like this is the everyday evidence for what the pact of Theodemir describes in words: a takeover negotiated with a population and an administration that largely stayed in place. CC BY-SA 2.5.

sectionImages.section: The Gothic claim, and a nationalist misuse
sectionImages.caption: The opening folio of Isidore's Etymologiae in a ninth-century copy written in Visigothic minuscule, the Codex Toletanus.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Iberian scribe, Toledo-Seville school
sectionImages.note: Biblioteca Nacional de España, Vitr. 14-3. Isidore's encyclopaedia was among the most copied books of the Middle Ages, and his History of the Goths opens with the Laus Spaniae — the praise of Spain as a patria on which later Iberian claims to the Gothic inheritance were built. Public domain.
